stories.title: Some half of Russian POWs interviewed by UN report torture in Ukraine
stories.summary: All prisoners of war must be treated humanely, UN Under-Secretary-General Rosemary DiCarlo said
article_sentences: Around half of Russian prisoners of war interviewed by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported torture and ill-treatment in the Ukrainian captivity, UN Under-Secretary-General Rosemary DiCarlo said, citing Russia’s official data.
"Approximately half of the Russian prisoners of war interviewed by OHCHR have provided accounts of torture or ill-treatment.
We remind the sides of their obligations under international humanitarian law.
All prisoners of war must be treated humanely," she said at a UN Security Council meeting convened by Western countries.
"We urge redoubled efforts to secure the release of all remaining captives, for their sake and for that of their families," she stressed.

stories.title: (Yonhap Interview) Korea's independence movement 'lofty cry' for universal values: historian
stories.summary: YANBIAN, China, Aug. 25 (Yonhap) -- Korea's struggle for independence from the J...
article_sentences: YANBIAN, China, Aug. 25 (Yonhap) -- Korea's struggle for independence from the Japanese colonial rule was a "lofty cry" for universal values, such as peace and humanitarianism, not merely a nationalist movement, a South Korean historian said.

Park Hwan, a scholar who has spent more than four decades researching Korea's independence movement during Japan's 1910-45 colonial rule, said the significance of the movement is often viewed too narrowly through a domestic lens.

"Many countries, including China, Russia, the United States, Mexico and even the Cuban government, supported Korea's independence movement," Park said in an interview with Yonhap News Agency during a recent tour to historic sites in Manchuria, now northeastern China.
"Korea's independence movement was not a movement solely for Koreans.
It was a struggle that pursued universal human values, including justice and humanitarianism," he said.
Park cautioned against viewing Korea's independence movement through a chauvinistic lens, saying such an approach could obscure the broader significance of the movement.

"The independence fighters issued a lofty call to the world in pursuit of peace and universal human values," he said, noting that many of them also joined forces with foreign advocates in China and Japan who opposed imperial Japan.

Park cited Ahn Jung-geun, the revered independence fighter who assassinated a senior Japanese colonial official in China 117 years ago, as a prime example of an independence activist whose vision extended beyond Korea to a broader pursuit of peace in East Asia.
"When asked about his final wish shortly before his execution on March 26, 1910, Ahn said he wanted to lead three cheers of 'long live peace in the East,'" Park said.

Before his execution by the Imperial Japanese Army at China's Lushun Prison, Ahn had been writing the "Theory of Peace in the East," a work arguing that Korea, China and Japan should coexist peacefully without invading one another and join forces to counter Western imperialism, according to Park.
Ahn died before completing the book.

Against the backdrop of the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine, which Park views as an early stage of a third world war, he said the ideals and values pursued by Korea's independence fighters remain relevant today and can help chart a course for the future.
